say: You give it $n$ objects and a number $r$. It counts the ways to pick $r$ of them **in order**, written $^nP_r$.
The key idea: each pick uses one object up, so the choices shrink by one each time. Multiply the $r$ shrinking numbers.

how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it on Paper 2, as a short 5-mark part on arranging letters or objects, or inside a longer counting question.

example.question: A club has $8$ members. A chairperson, a secretary and a treasurer are chosen, in that order. In how many ways can the three jobs be filled?

steps.title: Count the choices
steps.say: Fill the jobs one at a time. Eight people can be chairperson. That person is used up, so seven are left for secretary, then six for treasurer.

steps.title: Multiply the choices
steps.say: Order matters, so multiply the numbers of choices.

steps.title: Check with factorials
steps.say: The same count comes from the factorial formula for $^nP_r$.

ordinary.tip: Show the multiplication. If you list the factors and stop, the scheme still gives high partial credit.

say: You give it $P(A)$, $P(B)$ and $P(A \cap B)$. It gives you the probability of $A$ **or** $B$, $P(A \cup B)$.
The key idea: adding $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ counts the overlap twice, so take the overlap away once.

how.higher: Higher level uses it on Paper 2, often as a 5-mark part, to find a missing probability so that independence can be tested.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level uses it on Paper 2 in short 5-mark parts, usually to find the probability of one outcome or another from a table or list of outcomes.

example.question: $A$ and $B$ are events with $P(A) = \frac{3}{5}$, $P(B) = \frac{3}{10}$ and $P(A \cup B) = \frac{7}{10}$. Find $P(A \cap B)$. Hence state whether $A$ and $B$ are independent.

steps.title: Write the addition rule
steps.say: Start with the rule for $A$ or $B$. It has $P(A \cap B)$ in it, and that is what we want.

lines.tex: P(A \cup B) &= P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)

steps.title: Find the overlap
steps.say: Put the numbers in and make $\hl{1}{P(A \cap B)}$ the subject.

steps.title: Test for independence
steps.say: Independent events satisfy $P(A) \times P(B) = P(A \cap B)$. Multiply $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ and compare with $\hl{1}{\frac{1}{5}}$.

lines.text: They are not equal, so $A$ and $B$ are **not independent**.

workedSolution.finalAnswer: P(A \cap B) = \frac{1}{5}, \text{ so } A \text{ and } B \text{ are not independent}

higher.tip: Write the addition rule first. A correct relevant formula on its own earns partial credit.
To test independence, check $P(A) \times P(B) = P(A \cap B)$ with real values and finish with a conclusion.

say: You give it a list of stages, each with its probabilities. It draws a **tree** and gives the probability of any combined outcome.
The key idea: multiply along the branches to get one outcome, and add the outcomes you want.

how.higher: Higher level uses it on Paper 2 in most years, as a 10 or 15-mark part where you fill in a tree and then use it for a total or conditional probability.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level uses it on Paper 2 as a 10-mark part: complete or continue a tree, then multiply along branches to answer questions.

example.question: Sam takes two penalty kicks. The probability that he scores any one kick is $\frac{7}{10}$. Draw a tree diagram and find the probability that he scores at least one of the two kicks.

steps.title: Draw the branches
steps.say: Each kick has two branches: score ($S$) with $\frac{7}{10}$ and miss ($M$) with $\frac{3}{10}$. Both first-kick branches split again for the second kick.

lines.text: Second kick: the same two branches from each of those.

steps.title: Multiply along the branches
steps.say: The probability of one outcome is the product of the numbers along its branches.

steps.title: Add the outcomes you want
steps.say: At least one score means $S,S$ or $S,M$ or $M,S$. Add those three outcomes.

steps.title: Check with the opposite
steps.say: The only way to score none is $M,M$. Take $\hl{2}{\frac{9}{100}}$ away from $1$.

higher.tip: Fill in every branch. Marks go for each correct value, and values correct relative to your earlier ones are accepted.

say: You give it $n$ objects and a number $r$. It counts the ways to **choose** $r$ of them when order does not matter, written $^nC_r$.
The key idea: count the ordered picks, $^nP_r$, then divide by $r!$, because every group was counted $r!$ times.

how.higher: Higher level uses it on Paper 2 as a step inside bigger questions: counting selections, pairs or teams, or as the coefficient in a binomial probability.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it once, as a short part on Paper 2: how many ways can three of six be chosen.

example.question: In a game, $4$ numbers are chosen from the numbers $1$ to $15$, and the order does not matter. (i) How many different selections are possible? (ii) A player buys one ticket. Find the probability that it matches the chosen numbers.

steps.title: Use the formula
steps.say: Order does not matter, so this is a selection. Use $^nC_r = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}$ with $n = 15$ and $r = 4$.

steps.title: Cancel the factorials
steps.say: Cancel $11!$ from top and bottom. Four numbers are left on each side.

steps.title: Find the probability
steps.say: Only one of the $\hl{1}{1365}$ selections matches, so the probability is one over that.

higher.tip: Order of the pair may be treated either way, but be consistent. Mixing ordered and unordered in one question caps your marks.
